Several authors pair weakness with lowliness; al-Qāmūs, quoted by al-Biqāʿī, also lists it."}, {"id": "77:20/q03/p2", "position": "Lowly, contemptible, base, or insignificant.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba explicitly glosses it as lowly or contemptible; al-Māwardī reports Mujāhid and Qatāda, and al-Biqāʿī quotes al-Qāmūs. {"id": "77:20/q05", "question": "What response does recalling this origin call for or expose?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different, compatible lessons from the same reminder: humility, exposure of ingratitude, and obligation under divine lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "77:20/q05/p1", "position": "It should make humans reflect on their humble origin and restrain conceit.", "reasons": "Muqātil addresses deniers; al-Qushayrī says Adam's descendants claim more than other creatures despite their contemptible beginning."}, {"id": "77:20/q05/p2", "position": "It exposes ingratitude, disobedience, and defiant denial of God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls creation a blessing whose rejection makes ingratitude more heinous and punishment greater. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the passage reproaches arrogance toward worship and revelation."}, {"id": "77:20/q05/p3", "position": "God's sole lordship entails human submission and obligation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that creation and governance of human development prove sole lordship, and that lordship requires the creature's submission and obligation."}]}
{"id": "77:20/q06", "question": "What does the cited report say to a human who defies God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "77:20/q06/p1", "position": "God challenges Adam's child for defying Him after creation from such a humble substance.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr recalls the report from Busr ibn Jahhash in his discussion of Yā-Sīn."}]}
{"id": "77:20/q07", "question": "What does first creation establish about resurrection and judgment?", "turns_on": "The first line of argument establishes God's ability to recreate; the second draws the necessity of judgment from wisdom, provision, lordship, and moral awareness.", "positions": [{"id": "77:20/q07/p1", "position": "God's first creation of humans from insignificant fluid proves He can recreate the dead.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Iṣlāḥī, Kuran Yolu, and Study Quran make the inference. Al-Rāzī says denial of this evident proof warrants woe; Ibn Kathīr stresses the origin's insignificance beside God's power. Iṣlāḥī answers the objection of decayed bones by citing the already evident creation from mud and fluid; the fluid is ordinary and abundant. Kuran Yolu points to stages in the womb, the resulting material and spiritual powers, and humans as Earth's most perfect beings. Study Quran cites 32:8, 32:7, and 32:11."}, {"id": "77:20/q07/p2", "position": "The creative power, wisdom, providence, lordship, and moral order shown in human creation require a Day of Judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says sole lordship entails submission and obligation, hence recompense on the Day of Decision. Iṣlāḥī gives three further grounds: God's power, wisdom, and creativity in making humans; the elaborate provision system sustaining them; and innate awareness of good and evil. He also says human physical structure and stages of creation show power, providence, and wisdom, making resurrection certain and denial doomed."}]}
{"id": "77:20/q08", "question": "How does this reminder fit the surrounding passage and sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the local shift to creation as evidence or the wider alternation of reminders, warnings, and outcomes.", "positions": [{"id": "77:20/q08/p1", "position": "After warnings and historical evidence, the sūra turns to human creation as a stronger proof of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls this the third warning and relates its blessing to the gravity of unbelief. {"id": "77:21/q01", "question": "What does the pronoun in فَجَعَلْنَٰهُ refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "77:21/q01/p1", "position": "The reproductive water or fluid from which a child forms.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it water; al-Ṭabarī calls it weak fluid; al-Nasafī explicitly identifies the pronoun's referent as water; Ibn Kathīr speaks of male and female fluid gathered in the womb; al-Biqāʿī calls it a drop; Kur'an Yolu calls the despised water sperm and cites 75:37."}]}

{"id": "77:21/q06", "question": "What does human creation here establish?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different conclusions from creation: God's creative attributes and sole lordship, the possibility of recreation, and the necessity of a judgment that answers divine wisdom, governance, and moral obligation.", "positions": [{"id": "77:21/q06/p1", "position": "Resurrection is possible because God already created humans from humble fluid and can recreate them after death.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the stages of creation support resurrection because overwhelming divine power cannot be thwarted; the following praise reinforces this. {"id": "77:22/q01", "question": "What is the known appointed measure?", "turns_on": "Whether the measure names birth or the whole period to birth, a specified number of months, formation of the embryo, or the phases within gestation; the notes also differ on whether its length varies.", "positions": [{"id": "77:22/q01/p1", "position": "The divinely appointed span of pregnancy, ending at birth.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Wahidi-Wajiz, Baghawi, Qurtubi's unnamed explanation, Abu Hayyan, and Elmalili call it the time of birth; Wahidi-Basit gives both the duration and its endpoint, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Tabatabai call it the duration of pregnancy. {"id": "78:21/q13", "question": "When does Hell's ambush confront the rebellious?", "turns_on": "Whether the image is applied at death or at the resurrection scene.", "positions": [{"id": "78:21/q13/p1", "position": "At the Day of Decision, immediately after the world's upheaval.", "reasons": "Islahi says Hell appears after the destruction and raising of people, leaving rebels no time to prepare; Ibn Ashur locates the threat in the resurrection scene; Kuran Yolu says the preceding signs establish resurrection."}, {"id": "78:21/q13/p2", "position": "At death.", "reasons": "Study Quran says the rebels are ambushed then because they had been oblivious to truth in worldly life."}]}

{"id": "78:21/q15", "question": "How does the sentence attach to the preceding description of the Day?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause continues the syntax of 78:17 or independently answers what follows the Day's terrors.", "positions": [{"id": "78:21/q15/p1", "position": "It is a second predicate of the initial إن in 78:17, with an implied 'on that day'.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur relates a fixed appointment to a watch post as temporal marks for punishing rebels; the internal إن doubles the emphasis, as in a line by Jarir and 22:17, and completes what was said of people arriving in companies in 78:18."}, {"id": "78:21/q15/p2", "position": "It is an independent answer to the audience's implied question after the Day's horrors.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says this reading explains what follows those horrors and does not make al-taghin an unexpected turn in wording."}]}

{"id": "78:21/q17", "question": "Why does the passage present Hell first?", "turns_on": "The notes give different rhetorical effects of the sequence: priority of harm, warning the deniers, and clarifying later rewards.", "positions": [{"id": "78:21/q17/p1", "position": "The fearful outcome is presented before the benefit because averting harm has priority.", "reasons": "Biqai states this ordering principle."}, {"id": "78:21/q17/p2", "position": "The audience's denial of resurrection calls for a threat first.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites the occasion and the order of later statements; Kuran Yolu says the prior signs of resurrection lead into the deniers' afterlife. {"id": "78:22/q05", "question": "What does maʾāban mean here?", "turns_on": "The reports gloss the word as the place one returns to, as a dwelling or refuge, or as both; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the latter through metonymic usage.", "positions": [{"id": "78:22/q05/p1", "position": "A place of return, destination, or final outcome: Hell is where they come back.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī derive it from āba yaʾūbu, 'to return'; al-Naḥḥās cites a poem saying the dead do not return. {"id": "79:17/q05", "question": "Where do the reports place Pharaoh's origin?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted reports name Istakhr, Hamadan, or Isfahan; the notes do not decide between them.", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q05/p1", "position": "Pharaoh came from Istakhr.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this from Mujāhid."}, {"id": "79:17/q05/p2", "position": "Pharaoh was a non-Arab from Hamadan.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this from al-Ḥasan."}, {"id": "79:17/q05/p3", "position": "Pharaoh was from Isfahan.", "reasons": "A further report from al-Ḥasan in al-Qurṭubī calls him Dhū Ẓufr and says he stood four handspans tall."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q06", "question": "What does 'Pharaoh' designate here, and what was this ruler's situation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q06/p1", "position": "It is the title used for Moses' Egyptian king.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says Pharaoh was the title of Egypt's ancient Coptic kings, borrowed from Hebrew; the Qur'an uses it for Moses' ruler, whereas Joseph's ruler is called king, with 7:103 mentioned. Al-Biqāʿī calls him Egypt's king and says he enslaved Israel and feared an Israelite child; God raised Moses in Pharaoh's house as the means of his ruin, and Moses later fled after killing a man."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q07", "question": "What is the linguistic sense of 'ṭaghā' and related words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q07/p1", "position": "Ṭughyān is exceeding a limit.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī describes exceeding limits in corruption, compares baghy, and notes related forms for the act, agent, and transgressors. Al-Bursawī defines crossing the limit. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says Arabic applies it to dangerous overflowing water: 69:11 uses it for water, and al-ṭāghiya in 69:5 is glossed as Thamūd's destructive flood. She says most Qur'anic uses concern disobedience and disbelief, citing 2:15, 6:110, 7:186, 10:11, 23:71, 17:60, 5:64, 5:68, 38:55, and 78:22; she also cites 96:6, 89:11, 17:60, and 18:80 for tyranny, arrogance, and oppression."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q08", "question": "What verbal forms accompany the two forms of the present of 'ṭaghā'?", "turns_on": "The two Arabic usages differ in whether the present and past take the yāʾ or wāw stem.", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q08/p1", "position": "The present is yaṭghā, with past ṭaghaytu and verbal noun al-ṭughyān.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās assigns these forms to those who say yaṭghā."}, {"id": "79:17/q08/p2", "position": "The present is yaṭghū, with past ṭaghawtu.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās assigns ṭaghawtu to those who say yaṭghū."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q09", "question": "In what way had Pharaoh transgressed?", "turns_on": "The notes describe the bounds he crossed in general moral and religious terms or specify his demand for worship.", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q09/p1", "position": "He exceeded bounds through disbelief, corruption, arrogance, oppression, and disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī names disbelief; al-Baghawī adds pride and arrogance; al-Ṭabrisī adds rebellion and corruption; al-Qurṭubī names disobedience; al-Nasafī names unbelief and corruption. Al-Bursawī distinguishes disbelief against God from arrogance and enslavement against people, contrasting these with truth toward God and good character toward people. Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses excessive arrogance and compares 78:22. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes tyranny, arrogance, and oppression in Qur'anic usage."}, {"id": "79:17/q09/p2", "position": "His transgression reached the claim to be worshiped himself.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Pharaoh made himself an object of worship and called people to worship him. He also reports Ibn Masʿūd's reading that Pharaoh had never worshiped an idol but summoned people to worship himself."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q10", "question": "What does 'indeed, he transgressed' explain?", "turns_on": "Whether Pharaoh's transgression motivates the sending itself or Moses' obligation to obey the sending command.", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q10/p1", "position": "It gives the reason for the command to go.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī allow this reading; Ibn ʿĀshūr says opening with inna stresses the reason; Ṭabāṭabāʾī adopts it. Al-Biqāʿī connects the command to the recompense deserved by Pharaoh's transgression."}, {"id": "79:17/q10/p2", "position": "It gives the reason Moses must comply with the command.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī present this as the other possible attachment of the explanation."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q11", "question": "What does Pharaoh's conduct show about the origin of human acts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q11/p1", "position": "Human acts originate from the servants themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī argues this from Pharaoh's own transgression, denial, turning away, and calling out."}]}
{"id": "79:17/q12", "question": "What inward condition does Pharaoh's transgression exemplify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q12/p1", "position": "Egotism veiled him in selfhood and led to self-worship and tyranny.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī, reported by al-Bursawī, says Pharaoh's strength, wisdom, and learning did not prevent his claim to divine attributes and lordship. {"id": "79:17/q14", "question": "How does this command connect with the account in Ṭā Hā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:17/q14/p1", "position": "Ṭā Hā gives the parallel mission and adds the manner of invitation.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ points to 20:24 for the same command and declaration of transgression, and to 20:42–44 for Moses and Aaron's instruction to speak gently in hope that Pharaoh remembers or fears."}]}
